Record an access date when you actually consult a source. This repository does not imply every external page has been checked against the latest academic or certification requirement.

entries.title: Preparation
entries.text: Preparation Create a dedicated folder for lab records and synthetic files. Keep passwords, tokens, workplace information and personal data out of it. For Python labs, use Python 3 and its standard library. Run scripts from the directory containing your disposable files. For Linux labs, use an unprivileged account in a disposable VM or a local environment you control. The exercises below do not require sudo. For network labs, use Cisco Packet Tracer where provided by your course, or an equivalent approved simulator. Interface names vary: adapt GigabitEthernet0/0 and FastEthernet0/1 to the simulated device. Take a VM snapshot or save a separate simulator copy before a lab. A screenshot alone does not describe how to reproduce a result. Use the lab record template. Predict the result before executing a command.

entries.title: Lab 1 — Binary, hexadecimal, storage and validation
entries.text: Lab 1 — Binary, hexadecimal, storage and validation Units: Fundamentals of Computer Science; Computer Systems Architecture. Goal: perform calculations, state units and reject invalid inputs. Prerequisites: Python 3; a disposable working directory. Convert decimal 47 into binary and hexadecimal by hand. Show 32 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1. Predict the output of format(47, "08b"). Create representation.py: ```python def octet(value): if type(value) is not int or not 0 <= value <= 255: raise ValueError("an octet must be an integer from 0 to 255") return format(value, "08b"), format(value, "02X") assert octet(0) == ("00000000", "00") assert octet(47) == ("00101111", "2F") assert octet(255) == ("11111111", "FF") for invalid in (-1, 256, "47", True): try: octet(invalid) except ValueError: pass else: raise AssertionError(f"accepted invalid input: {invalid!r}") print("47:", octet(47)) print("1 GB in bytes:", 109) print("1 GiB in bytes:", 230) print("1 TB in TiB:", round(1012 / 2*40, 3)) ``` Run python representation.py. Extend the function to return decimal as well, keeping the validation. Add a boundary test rather than only retesting 47. Expected result: 47: 00101111 2F; GB and GiB are 1,000,000,000 and 1,073,741,824 bytes; 1 TB is approximately 0.909 TiB. All assertions pass. True is rejected deliberately: Python treats bool as a subclass of int, so the exact type check matters here. Evidence: hand conversion, script, test result and an explanation of one rejected input. Explain why a capacity-unit difference does not by itself prove storage is missing. Troubleshooting: AssertionError means a prediction or implementation is wrong; inspect the expected and actual values. If python is unavailable, use the interpreter name installed by your environment, often python3. Cleanup: delete only the lab files when no longer needed. Retain your explanation and test output.

entries.title: Lab 2 — Inventory reconciliation and algorithm choices
entries.text: Lab 2 — Inventory reconciliation and algorithm choices Units: Fundamentals of Computer Science; Professional Practice. Goal: validate structured data, detect duplicates and explain the algorithm. Prerequisites: Python 3; no external access. Create inventory.py with this synthetic fixture: ```python expected = {"LAB-SRV-01", "LAB-SRV-02", "LAB-SRV-03"} observed = ["LAB-SRV-01", "LAB-SRV-01", "LAB-SRV-03", "LAB-SRV-99"] seen = set() duplicates = set() for asset in observed: if asset in seen: duplicates.add(asset) seen.add(asset) missing = expected - seen unexpected = seen - expected assert missing == {"LAB-SRV-02"} assert unexpected == {"LAB-SRV-99"} assert duplicates == {"LAB-SRV-01"} print("Missing:", sorted(missing)) print("Unexpected:", sorted(unexpected)) print("Duplicates:", sorted(duplicates)) ``` Predict and run the output. Explain why converting the observed list into a set before checking duplicates would discard useful information. Add tests for an empty observed list, identical lists and a malformed identifier. Decide explicitly whether malformed data should stop processing or be reported separately. Compare repeated list membership checks with set membership. Explain average-case lookup assumptions and the memory trade-off; do not claim a runtime speedup without measuring it. Expected result: missing LAB-SRV-02, unexpected LAB-SRV-99, duplicate LAB-SRV-01. Evidence: tests, algorithm explanation and a short operational limitation: an absent identifier in a stale discovery file does not prove a physical asset is absent. Troubleshooting: sorting is used only to make display deterministic. Set iteration order must not be treated as a stable inventory order. Cleanup: keep synthetic fixtures only; do not substitute a real asset export without permission.

entries.title: Lab 3 — Hardware, capacity and power desk exercise
entries.text: Lab 3 — Hardware, capacity and power desk exercise Units: Computer Systems Architecture; Professional Practice. Goal: make a defensible comparison using specifications and calculations without opening equipment. Prerequisites: public manufacturer documentation for one chosen server or desktop model; calculator or Python. Build a table of CPU support, memory generation and maximum capacity, storage interfaces, form factor, PSU options, management features and relevant firmware revision. Record the exact model and document revision. Mark unavailable facts as unknown. For four equal 2 TB drives, calculate these simplified capacities: Layout Simplified usable capacity Important limitation RAID 0 across four drives 8 TB No drive-failure tolerance. RAID 1 using two mirrored pairs, presented separately Two 2 TB volumes; 4 TB total Failure tolerance depends on which drives fail. RAID 5 across four drives 6 TB Normally tolerates one drive failure; rebuild risk remains. RAID 6 across four drives 4 TB Normally tolerates two drive failures; controller support required. Ignore filesystem and metadata overhead for the calculation, then state that real usable space will be lower. Do not describe two separate mirrors as one large RAID 1 volume. 3. Calculate energy for a measured 400 W load over 24 hours: 0.4 kW × 24 h = 9.6 kWh. At an illustrative £0.25/kWh the result is £2.40. Calculate seven days and explain why maximum PSU rating is not a measured load. 4. A facility reports total energy of 120,000 kWh and IT-equipment energy of 80,000 kWh over the same boundary and period. Calculate PUE = 120,000 / 80,000 = 1.5. Explain why PUE alone cannot establish service efficiency or compare facilities with different measurement boundaries fairly. 5. Write a diagnostic decision tree for “powers on, no OS boot.” Separate firmware detection, boot order, drive presence, bootloader and OS symptoms. Include a point at which you stop and escalate. Expected result: correct capacity and energy arithmetic, source-specific compatibility claims and explicit assumptions. Evidence: comparison table, calculations with units, a diagnostic diagram and a paragraph distinguishing resilience from backup. Troubleshooting: mixed drive sizes and vendor RAID implementations change real capacity. Use the smallest-member capacity only when the specific layout's rules justify it. Avoid comparing products from marketing names alone. Cleanup: none; this lab involves no physical or configuration changes.

entries.title: Lab 4 — IPv4 subnetting and VLSM verification
entries.text: Lab 4 — IPv4 subnetting and VLSM verification Units: Core Networking; Fundamentals of Computer Science. Goal: produce an address plan and independently verify it. Prerequisites: Python 3; calculator optional. Addresses remain inside documentation or simulated examples. For 192.0.2.77/27, calculate network .64, broadcast .95, host range .65–.94, 32 total addresses and normally 30 hosts. Explain the 32-address block boundaries. Allocate 10.20.0.0/24 to segments requiring 60, 28 and 12 conventional host addresses. Include the gateway in each requirement or state how you count it. Allocate largest first: Segment Prefix Network Conventional usable range Broadcast A, up to 62 hosts /26 10.20.0.0 .1–.62 .63 B, up to 30 hosts /27 10.20.0.64 .65–.94 .95 C, up to 14 hosts /28 10.20.0.96 .97–.110 .111 Verify with Python: ```python from ipaddress import ip_interface, ip_network interface = ip_interface("192.0.2.77/27") print(interface.network) print(interface.network.broadcast_address) parent = ip_network("10.20.0.0/24") segments = [ip_network(x) for x in ( "10.20.0.0/26", "10.20.0.64/27", "10.20.0.96/28" )] assert all(segment.subnet_of(parent) for segment in segments) for i, segment in enumerate(segments): for other in segments[i + 1:]: assert not segment.overlaps(other) hosts = list(segment.hosts()) print(segment, hosts[0], hosts[-1], len(hosts)) ``` Deliberately replace segment C with 10.20.0.80/28. The overlap assertion should fail because that range sits within segment B. Restore the correct plan. Explain why the conventional 2^host_bits − 2 formula needs special treatment for /31 and /32. Do not use it blindly for all prefixes. Expected result: verified ranges above; an overlap produces an assertion failure. Evidence: hand calculation, verification output and one rejected overlapping plan with an explanation. Troubleshooting: ip_network rejects non-network addresses in strict mode. Do not silence this check merely to make an incorrect plan pass. Cleanup: restore the correct fixture or remove the disposable script.

entries.title: Lab 5 — IPv6 addressing and packet-path explanation
entries.text: Lab 5 — IPv6 addressing and packet-path explanation Unit: Core Networking. Goal: interpret prefixes and distinguish neighbour discovery from IPv4 ARP. Prerequisites: Python 3; optional two-host IPv6 simulator. 2001:db8::/32 is reserved for documentation. Expand 2001:db8:10::25 into eight groups: 2001:0db8:0010:0000:0000:0000:0000:0025. Assign two simulated hosts 2001:db8:10::10/64 and 2001:db8:10::20/64. Label their common prefix 2001:db8:10::/64. With Python, verify: python from ipaddress import ip_address, ip_network host = ip_address("2001:db8:10::25") print(host.exploded) assert host in ip_network("2001:db8:10::/64") assert host not in ip_network("2001:db8:20::/64") In the simulator, test host-to-host reachability and inspect neighbour discovery if the simulator exposes it. Explain how a host resolves an on-link neighbour and why IPv6 does not use IPv4 broadcast ARP. Explain the role of fe80::/10 link-local addresses and why a link-local address may need an interface scope identifier in a real OS. Expected result: the expanded address above and successful membership assertions; simulated hosts on the same link can communicate when the link and configuration are valid. Evidence: address plan, an annotated packet-path diagram and a comparison of IPv4 ARP and IPv6 neighbour discovery. Troubleshooting: a valid prefix alone does not establish connectivity; link state, duplicate addresses and host configuration still matter. Cleanup: close or reset the simulated topology; do not assign documentation addresses to an external interface.

entries.title: Lab 6 — VLANs, a trunk and inter-VLAN routing
entries.text: Lab 6 — VLANs, a trunk and inter-VLAN routing Units: Core Networking; Applied Networking. Goal: verify segmentation, then restore a controlled fault. Prerequisites: simulator; one router, one Layer 2 switch and two PCs. Use a fresh topology. Save a baseline copy. Connect PC-A to switch Fa0/1, PC-B to Fa0/2 and switch Gi0/1 to router Gi0/0. Use VLAN 10 for PC-A and VLAN 20 for PC-B. Configure PC-A as 192.0.2.10/26, gateway 192.0.2.1; PC-B as 192.0.2.70/26, gateway 192.0.2.65. On the simulated switch, adapt interface names if necessary: text enable configure terminal vlan 10 name LAB_A exit vlan 20 name LAB_B exit interface fastethernet0/1 switchport mode access switchport access vlan 10 spanning-tree portfast exit interface fastethernet0/2 switchport mode access switchport access vlan 20 spanning-tree portfast exit interface gigabitethernet0/1 switchport mode trunk switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20 end show vlan brief show interfaces trunk PortFast is used only on the two end-host ports in this isolated exercise. Do not enable it indiscriminately on links between switches. Some simulated models require explicit trunk encapsulation; consult that model's syntax. On the simulated router: text enable configure terminal interface gigabitethernet0/0 no shutdown exit interface gigabitethernet0/0.10 encapsulation dot1Q 10 ip address 192.0.2.1 255.255.255.192 exit interface gigabitethernet0/0.20 encapsulation dot1Q 20 ip address 192.0.2.65 255.255.255.192 end show ip interface brief show ip route From each PC, ping its own gateway and then the other PC. An initial packet may be lost during address resolution; repeat the test and explain the dependency. Predict what happens if the trunk carries only VLAN 10. In the simulator, change the allowed list to 10, test both PCs and capture the result. Restore switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20, retest and verify that the gateway and cross-VLAN tests recover. Expected result: the router has connected routes for 192.0.2.0/26 and 192.0.2.64/26; both VLANs appear on the trunk. Removing VLAN 20 breaks PC-B's routed path while VLAN 10 remains available. Evidence: topology, address/port plan, selected show output, before/fault/recovery test matrix and a packet-path explanation. Explain that the router permits inter-VLAN traffic here because no policy has yet been applied. Troubleshooting: check port state, cable, VLAN membership, trunk list, subinterface tag, mask and gateway before changing routing. A host in the wrong VLAN may have a correct-looking IP address but no valid gateway path. Cleanup: restore the baseline or keep a separate clearly named completed lab file. Never copy this configuration to real equipment.

entries.title: Lab 7 — Access control and positive/negative tests
entries.text: Lab 7 — Access control and positive/negative tests Unit: Applied Networking. Goal: show that a policy works in both directions of the requirement. Prerequisites: completed simulator topology from Lab 6. Save a separate copy. The policy is deliberately narrow: block ICMP echo requests from PC-A to PC-B, while allowing other IP traffic in this small lab. It is not a recommended production policy. Confirm PC-A can ping PC-B before applying the policy. On the simulated router: text configure terminal ip access-list extended LAB_A_IN deny icmp host 192.0.2.10 host 192.0.2.70 echo permit ip any any exit interface gigabitethernet0/0.10 ip access-group LAB_A_IN in end show access-lists show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0.10 Test PC-A → PC-B ping: it should fail. Test PC-A → its gateway: it should succeed. Test PC-B → PC-A ping: it should succeed because the returning echo reply from PC-A does not match the denied echo-request type. Inspect ACL counters after the tests. Explain direction: in means entering the router through VLAN 10's subinterface, not “towards PC-A.” Explain the implicit deny at the end of an ACL and why the final permit line matters in this exercise. Do not infer stateful firewall behaviour from this stateless ACL. Roll back: text configure terminal interface gigabitethernet0/0.10 no ip access-group LAB_A_IN in exit no ip access-list extended LAB_A_IN end Expected result: the three tests match the policy above; PC-A → PC-B ping works again after rollback. Exact counters depend on repeat count and simulator behaviour. Evidence: a test matrix with source, destination, protocol/type, expected, actual and interpretation; relevant ACL output; rollback verification. Troubleshooting: an ACL applied to the wrong interface or direction may never match. A failed positive test might come from routing or addressing rather than the ACL. Establish the baseline first. Cleanup: remove the ACL and verify baseline connectivity, or revert the saved lab copy.

entries.title: Lab 8 — Route selection and a troubleshooting runbook
entries.text: Lab 8 — Route selection and a troubleshooting runbook Units: Core Networking; Applied Networking; Professional Practice. Goal: explain longest-prefix match and build a diagnostic sequence. Prerequisites: paper or a text editor; optional simulator with three routers. Given the following hypothetical routes, determine the match for each destination before considering route-source preference: text 0.0.0.0/0 via 10.0.0.1 10.30.0.0/16 via 10.0.0.2 10.30.40.0/24 via 10.0.0.3 10.30.40.128/25 via 10.0.0.4 Expected matches: 10.30.40.150 → /25; 10.30.40.20 → /24; 10.30.80.20 → /16; 198.51.100.20 → default route. Assume the routes are installed and next hops are reachable; those assumptions need verification in a real network. Write a runbook for “client cannot reach service.” For each step state a test, expected result and branch: - link and interface state; - host address, prefix and gateway; - local gateway reachability; - forward and return route; - relevant ACL/firewall path; - transport listener and service health; - DNS compared with direct-address access. If building a simulator topology, introduce only one fault at a time: wrong host gateway, missing route or disabled interface. Ask another learner to diagnose it using your runbook. Expected result: correct prefix matches and a runbook that narrows faults without immediately changing configuration. Evidence: route reasoning, runbook, fault timeline and final recovery test. Distinguish a timeout from proof that a specific intermediate device is faulty. Troubleshooting: administrative distance and metric help select among route candidates for the same prefix; they do not make a less-specific installed route beat a more-specific match for forwarding. Cleanup: revert simulator faults and verify the saved baseline.

entries.title: Lab 9 — Linux files, permissions, backup and restore
entries.text:
Lab 9 — Linux files, permissions, backup and restore Units: Operating Systems; Professional Practice. Goal: explain permissions and prove recovery using disposable data. Prerequisites: Linux shell, mktemp, tar, sha256sum; unprivileged account. Run the commands in one subshell so the temporary variables and umask do not affect later work. ( lab_dir=$(mktemp -d -t az4caf-files-XXXXXX) || exit 1 trap 'rm -rf -- "$lab_dir"' EXIT umask 027 mkdir "$lab_dir/original" "$lab_dir/restored" printf 'Synthetic service configuration
port=8080
' > "$lab_dir/original/service.conf" chmod 640 "$lab_dir/original/service.conf" stat -c '%a %n' "$lab_dir/original/service.conf" tar -cf "$lab_dir/backup.tar" -C "$lab_dir/original" service.conf tar -tf "$lab_dir/backup.tar" tar -xf "$lab_dir/backup.tar" -C "$lab_dir/restored" sha256sum "$lab_dir/original/service.conf" "$lab_dir/restored/service.conf" cmp "$lab_dir/original/service.conf" "$lab_dir/restored/service.conf" && printf 'Restore content matches
' ) Predict what 640 allows: owner read/write; group read; others no permission. Explain why directory execute permission has a different meaning from file execute permission. Run the commands and interpret the two matching hashes. The archive contains only the disposable configuration file created in this lab. Repeat in a new disposable directory, modify the restored file and show that cmp detects a mismatch. Restore again and verify recovery. State what the test establishes: content equality for one file. It does not establish a full system restore, preserved ACLs, application consistency or achievement of an RPO/RTO. Expected result: permission 640, archive member service.conf, matching SHA-256 values and Restore content matches. Evidence: interpreted permission output, hashes and scope/limitations. Measure elapsed restore time if practising RTO calculations, stating what the measurement includes. Troubleshooting: a missing command indicates a platform difference; use an approved environment rather than changing system packages without need. Do not extract an untrusted archive with these commands. Cleanup: the trap deletes only the directory created by mktemp. Do not replace it with a broad directory path or run cleanup against your evidence folder.

entries.title: Lab 10 — A local service: running, listening and reachable
entries.text: Lab 10 — A local service: running, listening and reachable Units: Operating Systems; Applied Networking. Goal: distinguish process state, socket state and an application response. Prerequisites: Python 3; two terminal sessions; local port 8765 available. In terminal A create a disposable directory, put a file named health.txt in it containing lab-ok, and start a loopback-only server from that directory: bash python -m http.server 8765 --bind 127.0.0.1 The server exposes files in its current directory to local clients. Use only the disposable directory. 2. In terminal B request the file without requiring curl: bash python -c "from urllib.request import urlopen; print(urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8765/health.txt', timeout=3).read().decode().strip())" On Linux, inspect the listener using ss -ltn and find 127.0.0.1:8765. If ss is unavailable, use the OS's documented socket tool. Explain why binding to loopback limits reachability. Request a missing filename and observe an HTTP 404 in the server log. Explain how this differs from a connection refusal when no process is listening. Stop the server with Ctrl+C in terminal A and repeat the valid request. It should fail because the listening process has ended. Expected result: lab-ok while the server is running; an HTTP 404 for a missing file; a connection failure after shutdown. Exact exception wording varies by OS. Evidence: a dependency diagram, listener output and three outcomes. Explain why “process running” is weaker evidence than a successful application request. Troubleshooting: “address already in use” means another listener uses the port. Choose another unused high port consistently; do not terminate an unfamiliar process. If a request fails while the server is running, compare address, port, filename and working directory. Cleanup: stop the server and remove only the disposable files you created. Confirm the listener has gone.

entries.title: Lab 11 — Windows process and recovery practice
entries.text: Lab 11 — Windows process and recovery practice Unit: Operating Systems. Goal: practise read-only inspection and file recovery with PowerShell. Prerequisites: Windows with PowerShell; unprivileged account. No services or system configuration are changed. $labDir = Join-Path ([System.IO.Path]::GetTempPath()) ("az4caf-" + [guid]::NewGuid().ToString()) New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $labDir | Out-Null try { $original = Join-Path $labDir "original.txt" $backup = Join-Path $labDir "backup.txt" $restored = Join-Path $labDir "restored.txt" Set-Content -Path $original -Value "Synthetic configuration" -Encoding UTF8 Copy-Item -Path $original -Destination $backup Copy-Item -Path $backup -Destination $restored Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -Path $original, $restored Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 Name, Id, CPU } finally { Remove-Item -LiteralPath $labDir -Recurse -Force } Compare hashes and explain why copying files is only a small recovery exercise. Interpret CPU as accumulated processor time for the process, not the current CPU utilisation percentage. Explain why two observations at different times can differ. Use Get-Service | Select-Object -First 10 Name, Status for read-only service inspection. Do not stop or reconfigure unfamiliar services. Compare the terms process, service, listening port and application response with Lab 10. Expected result: matching content hashes; process and service lists reflect the local machine. Do not publish personally identifying paths or process details unnecessarily. Evidence: a short interpretation using only approved, relevant output. Redact personal path details from screenshots. Troubleshooting: shell versions and permissions affect available fields. A blank CPU value does not mean a process has never used CPU; access restrictions or unavailable data may apply. Cleanup: the finally block removes the new temporary directory. Do not alter it to point at an existing folder.

entries.title: Lab 12 — AI evaluation without a training framework
entries.text: Lab 12 — AI evaluation without a training framework Units: Core AI; Fundamentals of Computer Science. Goal: calculate metrics, compare a baseline and explain operational consequences. Prerequisites: Python 3; synthetic labels only. Treat 1 as “requires investigation” and 0 as “does not require investigation.” Create metrics.py: ```python actual = [1] * 12 + [0] * 88 predicted = [1] * 8 + [0] * 4 + [1] * 2 + [0] * 86 def metrics(truth, guess): if len(truth) != len(guess) or not truth: raise ValueError("non-empty label lists must have equal length") if any(value not in (0, 1) for value in truth + guess): raise ValueError("this exercise expects binary labels") tp = sum(t == 1 and p == 1 for t, p in zip(truth, guess)) fp = sum(t == 0 and p == 1 for t, p in zip(truth, guess)) fn = sum(t == 1 and p == 0 for t, p in zip(truth, guess)) tn = sum(t == 0 and p == 0 for t, p in zip(truth, guess)) precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else None recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else None accuracy = (tp + tn) / len(truth) return tp, fp, fn, tn, precision, recall, accuracy result = metrics(actual, predicted) assert result[:4] == (8, 2, 4, 86) print("Candidate:", result) print("Always negative:", metrics(actual, [0] * len(actual))) ``` Calculate the results by hand before running it: precision 80%, recall about 66.7%, accuracy 94%. The always-negative baseline has 88% accuracy and 0% recall; precision is undefined because it predicts no positive cases. Explain why the code uses None rather than pretending the ratio is meaningful. Use illustrative costs of £100 per false negative and £5 per false positive. Candidate error cost: 4×£100 + 2×£5 = £410; always-negative cost: 12×£100 = £1,200. Explain that these assumed costs are a teaching example, not evidence of real business savings. Design a data split for six months of timestamped events: earlier months for training, a later period for validation and the final period held out for testing. Explain why random splitting can leak future operational patterns. List leakage risks: post-resolution labels in input features, duplicates spanning splits, preprocessing fitted on all data and selecting the final model based on the test set. Expected result: confusion counts and baseline above. This lab evaluates supplied predictions; it does not train a model or establish performance on unseen operational data. Evidence: hand calculations, output, a split diagram, a cost discussion and a limitation statement. State which decision remains with a human. Troubleshooting: swapping the meanings of positive and negative changes precision and recall. Define the positive class before calculating. Cleanup: delete the synthetic script if desired. Do not replace the fixture with workplace telemetry without approval.

entries.title: Lab 13 — AI-assisted explanation with verification
entries.text: Lab 13 — AI-assisted explanation with verification Units: Core AI; Professional Practice. Goal: evaluate an assistant's output as a claim that needs evidence. Prerequisites: an approved AI tool if available; otherwise use a peer-written answer. Use only a fictional scenario. Ask for a troubleshooting explanation for a synthetic host that can reach its gateway but cannot resolve a hostname. Separate the response into facts, assumptions, hypotheses and proposed actions. Mark any invented environmental details. Verify two technical claims against the exact OS or vendor documentation. Record the section and access date. Reject any proposed action that changes unrelated infrastructure, exposes secrets or exceeds the stated scope. Rewrite the advice into read-only tests first. Produce your own final explanation, including uncertainties and the next test that would distinguish a DNS problem from a broader service issue. Expected result: an evidence-based critique, not a screenshot showing that a tool produced fluent text. Evidence: synthetic prompt, relevant output excerpts where permitted, claim/source table and your corrected explanation. Follow your institution's AI-use and attribution rules. Troubleshooting: a link in generated output may be nonexistent or irrelevant. Open the authoritative document and confirm what it supports. Cleanup: remove any accidentally included sensitive content according to the tool and institutional process; prevent it by using synthetic data from the start.

entries.title: Lab 14 — Incident handover and change rehearsal
entries.text: Lab 14 — Incident handover and change rehearsal Units: Professional Practice; Work Based Learning; Applied Networking. Goal: communicate an operational problem and practise a controlled response. Prerequisites: Lab 6 simulator or a tabletop exercise with a peer. No workplace data. Scenario: at 10:00 UTC a simulated host in VLAN 20 loses gateway connectivity after an approved lab change. VLAN 10 still works. The previous saved configuration carried both VLANs; the current trunk carries VLAN 10 only. Write a brief incident update with impact, start time, facts, hypothesis, owner and next update time. Label the missing VLAN as a hypothesis until verified. Collect the trunk and interface outputs. State what each supports and what remains unknown. Prepare a change plan to restore VLAN 20. Include a pre-change snapshot, expected impact, positive and negative tests, rollback steps and a measurable stop condition. Have a peer review the plan. In a tabletop exercise, role-play approval; do not imply that a classroom role-play grants workplace permission. Apply the correction only in the simulator. Verify both VLANs and record the result. Write a handover another learner could use without asking you to repeat the history. Include current state, evidence references and remaining actions. Reflect on the process: was the fault detection timely, was the change scope clear and did the communication distinguish facts from assumptions? Expected result: a reproducible plan, successful simulator recovery and a concise factual handover. A peer can explain the next action and its owner. Evidence: incident timeline, change plan, selected outputs, test matrix and reflection. Use the templates. Troubleshooting: avoid rewriting the initial record to make your first hypothesis look correct. Preserve the original hypothesis and add the test result. Cleanup: restore or save the intended lab baseline; close the simulated incident record as a training exercise.

entries.title: Lab 15 — Placement learning plan or optional project proposal
entries.text: Lab 15 — Placement learning plan or optional project proposal Units: Work Based Learning; Professional Practice; optional Designing a Computing Project. Goal: prepare an achievable learning activity with evidence and boundaries. Prerequisites: current tutor guidance. Placement availability and project approval are separate institutional decisions. Placement practice route Draft three objectives with observable outcomes, such as “explain an approved incident escalation path using a supervisor-reviewed anonymised flowchart.” For each objective list authorised activities, required supervision, evidence permitted by the host, a review date and a fallback if the activity is unavailable. Draft one learning-log entry using a fictional observation. Label it “practice example”; do not submit it as workplace evidence. Explain how you will distinguish observing, assisting and performing under supervision. Agree actual evidence arrangements with HRUC and the placement host before collecting workplace material. Optional project practice route Obtain the current Pearson-set theme and tutor-approved brief before choosing the assessed project. As a practice proposal, consider a local synthetic incident-log analyser. Define users, inputs, outputs and success criteria, such as rejecting malformed timestamps and reproducing a supplied count exactly. Plan research, design, implementation, evaluation and reporting milestones. Add risks, ethical issues and scope exclusions. Create a synthetic dataset with known expected results and a test plan before implementation. Explain how you will evaluate the outcome honestly, including an unmet criterion or limitation. Expected result: a plan that can be reviewed and revised, with clear boundaries and measurable outcomes. It is not a completed assessment or a guarantee of Level 5 progression. Evidence: proposal, objective/evidence matrix, schedule, risk register and tutor feedback where appropriate. Troubleshooting: an objective such as “learn networking” is too broad; narrow it to a concept, activity and observable result. Do not promise access to production systems as a project dependency. Cleanup: replace practice placeholders only after approval; retain version history so scope changes are visible.

entries.title: Lab 16 — Linux access and a read-only diagnostic baseline
entries.text: Lab 16 — Linux access and a read-only diagnostic baseline Units: Operating Systems; Applied Networking; Professional Practice. Goal: establish approved access and explain what a diagnostic baseline shows. Prerequisites: a disposable Linux VM or local Linux environment you control. For SSH, the VM must already have a configured SSH service and an individually assigned account. Confirm the expected host-key fingerprint through the VM console or another trusted channel. Do not install or expose an SSH server on a public interface for this exercise. First practise locally. Record identity and environment without displaying secrets: bash id hostname uname -r pwd uptime df -h . free -h ps -u "$(id -u)" -o pid,comm,etime Explain real versus effective identity if the environment distinguishes them. df -h . reports the filesystem containing the working directory; it is not an inventory of every physical drive. Available memory includes reclaimable resources, so “free” memory alone is not a complete memory-pressure assessment. 2. On the disposable VM, use ip address and ip route to identify the intended lab interface and route. Record only relevant output. If the host has other interfaces, do not change or probe them. 3. If approved SSH access is available, connect with the assigned account, substituting the real address of your own isolated VM: bash ssh labuser@192.168.56.10 192.168.56.10 is an example private address, not a service provided by this repository. Use only the address assigned to your VM. Confirm the presented fingerprint against the trusted value before accepting it. Do not disable host-key checking to bypass a mismatch. 4. On the remote session run id, hostname and pwd again. Explain which machine produced each result. If the shell prompt alone is ambiguous, include an explicit hostname in your evidence. 5. Inspect your own files and permissions with ls -ld . and ls -l. Use a dedicated lab directory rather than listing another person's files. Explain why login success does not grant permission for every operation. 6. If the VM uses systemd, run the read-only command systemctl --failed. An empty failure list means systemd reports no units in the failed state at that moment; it does not prove every application is healthy. Use Lab 10 to demonstrate the separate need for an application-level check. 7. End the remote session with exit. Confirm that a subsequent hostname comes from the local environment. Expected result: the intended individual account accesses the intended VM; diagnostic output can be explained; the session closes cleanly. Results such as memory size, uptime and process count depend on the VM. Evidence: a short baseline table with timestamp, machine, command, observation and interpretation. Redact personal usernames, internal hostnames and addresses where required. State that this is lab evidence, not workplace access. Troubleshooting: connection refusal suggests no listener at that address/port; a timeout can have several causes, including routing or filtering; authentication failure does not imply a network fault. A host-key change must be investigated through a trusted channel. Do not delete the known-host entry merely to make the warning disappear. Cleanup: close SSH sessions; remove disposable lab files only. If the VM is no longer needed, shut it down or revert its snapshot using the normal VM controls. Do not remove keys or change account privileges outside the agreed lab scope.

entries.title: Extended tools and complex networks
entries.text: Extended tools and complex networks Use the data-tools guide for the detailed Access, MongoDB, Python and Node pathway, including local examples and access boundaries. Use the network-labs guide for deeper switch configuration, firewalls and complex network topologies. These focused guides extend the sequence above without changing the official unit list. For every extension keep the same evidence discipline: define a working baseline, predict a result, collect actual output, test allowed and denied behaviour where relevant, document limitations and verify cleanup. An application that connects successfully with one account has not automatically proved least privilege for other operations.

entries.title: Integrated challenge — investigate, restore and explain
entries.text: Integrated challenge — investigate, restore and explain Combine the skills above in a fresh copy of your simulator and local fixtures: Produce an address plan and inventory for a two-VLAN training environment. Establish and document a working baseline. Ask a peer to introduce one agreed reversible simulator fault. Do not reveal its cause to the investigator. Diagnose with read-only tests, recording predictions and results. Propose and review the smallest correction that addresses the evidence. Restore service, verify unaffected behaviour and record rollback readiness. Write a technical report and a short non-technical incident update. Summarise the evidence in a synthetic CSV and explain one simple metric. If using AI assistance, verify the output and attribute its use according to your institution's policy. Evaluate the work against reproducibility, correct reasoning, verified recovery, clear communication and honest limitations. These are study criteria, not an official assessment rubric.

entries.title: Reading alongside the labs
entries.text: Reading alongside the labs Use the authoritative starting references, the notes' source links, and the manuals for your actual tool versions. Particularly useful references include Python ipaddress, Python HTTP server, Microsoft PowerShell documentation, Cisco support and NIST AI RMF. Record the access date when you consult a source. A successful simulator lab demonstrates behaviour in that simulator; explain its limits before generalising to real hardware or operational practice.

entries.title: Working method and prerequisites
entries.text: Working method and prerequisites Use an isolated Packet Tracer project for the Cisco exercises. The examples assume two Catalyst 2960-style Layer 2 switches and two ISR 2911-style routers. Interface names, crypto capabilities and simulator support vary. A real IOS image, different switch family or another simulator may need different syntax. Check the device help and its own official guide before adapting a command. For Linux exercises, use a disposable Linux VM with iproute2, nftables, Python 3, curl and optionally tcpdump/DNS tools installed. Namespace creation requires administrative rights. These exercises configure only named lab namespaces; do not run them on workplace equipment or a shared host. For every change: Draw the intended path and record the current state. Keep console access or another known working management path. Change one dependency at a time and verify it before continuing. Save a known working checkpoint; keep the previous file for rollback. Record actual commands and observations, including unsuccessful tests. A successful ping alone does not establish that DNS, application access, segmentation and recovery all work. Test required flows and prohibited flows.

entries.title: 1. The topology and address plan
entries.text: 1. The topology and address plan User PC SW1 R1 R2 10.44.0.10/26 -- Fa0/1 Gi0/1 -- trunk -- G0/0 G0/1 -- /30 -- G0/0 | | Fa0/23 + Fa0/24 G0/1 LACP Port-channel1 | | Remote PC .194/27 SW2 / | \ Fa0/1 Fa0/2 Fa0/3 Server Admin Storage test host .70/26 .164/28 .130/27 Both switches have VLANs 10, 20, 30, 99 and 999. SW1 connects the router trunk; the two member links between switches form one logical LACP trunk. VLAN 999 is an unused native/parking VLAN without a gateway or management address. There is no separate physical firewall in this first topology: the router routes, and a later ACL demonstrates a limited stateless filter. The Linux exercise then demonstrates a stateful firewall separately. Purpose VLAN Network/prefix Mask Usable range Broadcast Gateway Users 10 10.44.0.0/26 255.255.255.192 .1–.62 .63 .1 Servers 20 10.44.0.64/26 255.255.255.192 .65–.126 .127 .65 Storage lab 30 10.44.0.128/27 255.255.255.224 .129–.158 .159 .129 Management 99 10.44.0.160/28 255.255.255.240 .161–.174 .175 .161 R1–R2 transit — 10.44.0.176/30 255.255.255.252 .177–.178 .179 — Remote branch — 10.44.0.192/27 255.255.255.224 .193–.222 .223 .193 Addresses .180–.191 and .224–.255 remain unallocated; they are not one continuous free subnet. R1 uses transit .177 and R2 uses .178. SW1 management is .162 and SW2 is .163. All abbreviated addresses in this table begin 10.44.0. Worked VLSM checks A /26 leaves six host bits: 2^6 = 64 addresses, ordinarily 62 usable host addresses. The increments are 64, so .70/26 belongs to .64/26, not .0/26. Its gateway .65 is inside the same subnet. .127 is the broadcast address and cannot be allocated to the server. A /28 leaves four host bits: 16 addresses and ordinarily 14 usable hosts. .164/28 falls in the block .160–.175. The admin host, .161 gateway, .162 SW1 and .163 SW2 therefore share VLAN 99's subnet. A /30 leaves two host bits: .176 network, .177 and .178 hosts, .179 broadcast. /31 point-to-point addressing is possible on supporting equipment, but this lab deliberately uses /30. Allocate larger required subnets first, align each network to its block boundary, then check that ranges do not overlap. Count interfaces, gateways and future capacity as well as end devices. Evidence: an annotated topology, a complete address table and calculations for one subnet of each size. Explain why a VLAN number does not determine an IP subnet.

entries.title: 2. Establish a switch baseline and management access
entries.text: 2. Establish a switch baseline and management access Connect through the console. Confirm the device/interface names with show version and show interfaces status. In Packet Tracer choose private, unique lab passwords when entering these commands; angle-bracket values below are placeholders and must be replaced. On SW1: enable configure terminal hostname SW1 no ip domain-lookup enable secret <choose-a-unique-lab-enable-secret> username labadmin privilege 15 secret <choose-a-different-lab-secret> ip domain-name az4caf.example crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048 ip ssh version 2 line console 0 logging synchronous exec-timeout 10 0 login local exit line vty 0 15 login local transport input ssh exec-timeout 10 0 exit vlan 10 name USERS vlan 20 name SERVERS vlan 30 name STORAGE_LAB vlan 99 name MANAGEMENT vlan 999 name PARKING_NATIVE exit interface vlan 99 ip address 10.44.0.162 255.255.255.240 no shutdown exit ip default-gateway 10.44.0.161 end Repeat on SW2, changing the hostname and SVI address to 10.44.0.163. Some simulator images prompt for the RSA modulus instead of accepting it on the same line; use the platform-supported equivalent. Do not substitute Telnet on a production network if a simulator lacks SSH. An SVI can remain down until that VLAN exists and an appropriate Layer 2 port is active and forwarding. At this stage no remote gateway is configured on R1, so routed SSH access is not expected yet. ip default-gateway is for this Layer 2 switch's own management traffic. It does not enable inter-VLAN routing. On a Layer 3 switch running ip routing, use the appropriate routed/default route design instead. The privilege 15 account is a lab convenience. In operations, use approved role-based accounts, AAA, central authentication and emergency access controls. Never publish secrets, private keys or full sensitive configurations as assignment evidence. Verify: show vlan brief show ip interface brief show ip ssh show running-config Expected: the VLANs exist, the management address is correct, and VTY access allows SSH. Record whether the SVI is up and explain the dependencies.

entries.title: 3. Configure access ports and the router trunk
entries.text: 3. Configure access ports and the router trunk On SW1 configure the user port and router-facing trunk: configure terminal interface fastethernet 0/1 description LAB_USER_PC switchport mode access switchport access vlan 10 spanning-tree portfast spanning-tree bpduguard enable no shutdown exit interface gigabitethernet 0/1 description TRUNK_TO_R1_G0_0 switchport mode trunk switchport trunk native vlan 999 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30,99,999 switchport nonegotiate no shutdown end On SW2: configure terminal interface fastethernet 0/1 description LAB_SERVER switchport mode access switchport access vlan 20 spanning-tree portfast spanning-tree bpduguard enable no shutdown exit interface fastethernet 0/2 description LAB_ADMIN switchport mode access switchport access vlan 99 spanning-tree portfast spanning-tree bpduguard enable no shutdown exit interface fastethernet 0/3 description LAB_STORAGE_HOST switchport mode access switchport access vlan 30 spanning-tree portfast spanning-tree bpduguard enable no shutdown end PortFast and BPDU Guard here are for known endpoint access ports. Do not apply this edge configuration blindly to switch uplinks. Receiving a BPDU can disable an edge port under BPDU Guard; investigate the unexpected bridge before recovery. Some switches require switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q; 2960 platforms with only 802.1Q do not offer that command. A command rejected because the platform differs is evidence to investigate, not a reason to paste larger configuration blocks repeatedly. For unused access ports, select only ports that are genuinely unused, put them in VLAN 999 and administratively shut them down. Keep the selected uplinks and console path available.

entries.title: 4. Build the LACP inter-switch trunk
entries.text: 4. Build the LACP inter-switch trunk Cable SW1 Fa0/23 to SW2 Fa0/23 and SW1 Fa0/24 to SW2 Fa0/24. Start from unconfigured lab ports. On both switches: configure terminal interface range fastethernet 0/23 - 24 description LACP_MEMBERS_TO_OTHER_SWITCH switchport mode trunk switchport trunk native vlan 999 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30,99,999 switchport nonegotiate channel-group 1 mode active no shutdown exit interface port-channel 1 description LACP_TRUNK_TO_OTHER_SWITCH switchport mode trunk switchport trunk native vlan 999 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30,99,999 no shutdown end LACP active/active negotiates; active/passive can negotiate; passive/passive does not initiate. Match native/allowed VLANs, speed, duplex and channel settings. Do not mix LACP with proprietary PAgP on the peer. Verify: show etherchannel summary show interfaces trunk show interfaces port-channel 1 Expected: Port-channel1 is Layer 2 and in use; both physical members are bundled. IOS commonly displays Po1(SU) and member (P) flags. Exact formatting varies. A suspended or standalone member is not a successful bundle. A two-link bundle can carry multiple flows across members according to a hash. It does not normally double the speed of one flow, and it does not survive loss of both switches. Record which failures it addresses and which remain single points of failure.

entries.title: 5. Set and inspect spanning tree
entries.text: 5. Set and inspect spanning tree On both switches: configure terminal spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst end On SW1: configure terminal spanning-tree vlan 10,20,30,99,999 priority 24576 end On SW2: configure terminal spanning-tree vlan 10,20,30,99,999 priority 28672 end Verify show spanning-tree vlan 10 and show spanning-tree vlan 99. SW1 should be the root with this isolated topology. Displayed bridge priorities may include the extended system ID (VLAN number), so VLAN 10 can display 24586 rather than 24576. The LACP members form one logical STP port. In this topology there is no extra standalone inter-switch link that STP needs to block. Do not manufacture a loop to test redundancy on physical equipment. Failure exercise: after saving a working checkpoint, shut down one channel member. The port-channel should remain up through the other member. Restore the member and confirm it rejoins. A brief transient or packet loss is possible; observe rather than promising zero interruption.

entries.title: 6. Configure router-on-a-stick gateways
entries.text: 6. Configure router-on-a-stick gateways On R1, G0/0 is connected to SW1's Gi0/1 trunk: enable configure terminal hostname R1 interface gigabitethernet 0/0 description DOT1Q_TRUNK_TO_SW1 no ip address no shutdown exit interface gigabitethernet 0/0.10 encapsulation dot1Q 10 ip address 10.44.0.1 255.255.255.192 exit interface gigabitethernet 0/0.20 encapsulation dot1Q 20 ip address 10.44.0.65 255.255.255.192 exit interface gigabitethernet 0/0.30 encapsulation dot1Q 30 ip address 10.44.0.129 255.255.255.224 exit interface gigabitethernet 0/0.99 encapsulation dot1Q 99 ip address 10.44.0.161 255.255.255.240 exit interface gigabitethernet 0/0.999 encapsulation dot1Q 999 native no ip address end Set endpoint IP addresses, masks and gateways from the address table. Initially allow routing between all lab VLANs to verify the foundation. Security policy is added after the path works. Verify: show ip interface brief show ip route connected show arp Test from the admin PC to .161, .162 and .163. Test the user PC's own gateway before testing .70 on the server VLAN. Test SSH to both switches from the admin PC. In Packet Tracer, a PC can use ssh -l labadmin 10.44.0.162 if its SSH client is supported. Explain the packet path: the user PC determines that .70 is outside its /26, ARPs for .1, sends a frame to R1's MAC, and R1 routes to VLAN 20. The destination IP remains .70 while Layer 2 addresses change at the routed boundary. Switches learn source MAC addresses; they do not route this packet merely because they have a management SVI. Design comparison: a multilayer switch could use SVIs and ip routing instead of router subinterfaces. This can remove the router trunk bottleneck, but changes the topology and routing responsibilities. Do not configure both designs with duplicate gateway addresses in the same live lab.

entries.title: 7. Add a routed branch with static routes
entries.text: 7. Add a routed branch with static routes Cable R1 G0/1 to R2 G0/0. Cable R2 G0/1 to the remote PC. On R1: configure terminal interface gigabitethernet 0/1 description TRANSIT_TO_R2 ip address 10.44.0.177 255.255.255.252 no shutdown exit ip route 10.44.0.192 255.255.255.224 10.44.0.178 end On R2: enable configure terminal hostname R2 interface gigabitethernet 0/0 description TRANSIT_TO_R1 ip address 10.44.0.178 255.255.255.252 no shutdown exit interface gigabitethernet 0/1 description REMOTE_LAN ip address 10.44.0.193 255.255.255.224 no shutdown exit ip route 10.44.0.0 255.255.255.192 10.44.0.177 ip route 10.44.0.64 255.255.255.192 10.44.0.177 ip route 10.44.0.128 255.255.255.224 10.44.0.177 ip route 10.44.0.160 255.255.255.240 10.44.0.177 end Give the remote PC .194/27 and gateway .193. Verify routes in both directions. The exact reverse routes make the return path explicit. A broad summary/default route can be valid in other designs, but can also create a loop or black hole if the next-hop design is wrong. Test the transit neighbor first, then remote gateway, then end-to-end traffic. Use traceroute on IOS or tracert on a simulated PC to investigate the path. Firewalls and control-plane rate limits can affect traceroute replies even when a service works.

entries.title: 8. Replace static routing with single-area OSPF
entries.text: 8. Replace static routing with single-area OSPF Save a separate checkpoint. This is an alternative to the static route exercise, not an extra reason for the existing statics to remain. Remove the exact static routes above with no ip route ..., using each complete route command. On R1: configure terminal no ip route 10.44.0.192 255.255.255.224 10.44.0.178 router ospf 1 router-id 1.1.1.1 passive-interface default no passive-interface gigabitethernet 0/1 network 10.44.0.0 0.0.0.63 area 0 network 10.44.0.64 0.0.0.63 area 0 network 10.44.0.128 0.0.0.31 area 0 network 10.44.0.160 0.0.0.15 area 0 network 10.44.0.176 0.0.0.3 area 0 end On R2: configure terminal no ip route 10.44.0.0 255.255.255.192 10.44.0.177 no ip route 10.44.0.64 255.255.255.192 10.44.0.177 no ip route 10.44.0.128 255.255.255.224 10.44.0.177 no ip route 10.44.0.160 255.255.255.240 10.44.0.177 router ospf 1 router-id 2.2.2.2 passive-interface default no passive-interface gigabitethernet 0/0 network 10.44.0.176 0.0.0.3 area 0 network 10.44.0.192 0.0.0.31 area 0 end The OSPF network statements select matching interfaces; they are not ordinary forwarding routes. The wildcard mask is the inverse of the subnet mask: /27 has 0.0.0.31. Passive interfaces advertise their attached networks without forming neighbors there. The transit interfaces are the intended neighbor adjacency. Verify: show ip ospf neighbor show ip ospf interface brief show ip protocols show ip route ospf Expected: the transit neighbor reaches FULL state. A broadcast Ethernet network can show a FULL/DR or FULL/BDR relationship. R1 learns the remote /27; R2 learns the four VLAN networks. Static routes left in place can hide the expected OSPF route because a normal static route has lower administrative distance. This two-router topology has no alternate routed path. OSPF does not create redundancy without another usable path. For an extension, add a third router, two separate transit subnets and another destination network. Draw all return paths, assign unique router IDs, establish adjacencies and compare route costs before testing link failure. Troubleshooting: check physical state, addressing/subnet, matching area, compatible hello/dead timers, authentication settings, passive status and filtering of OSPF before changing routing statements at random. Optional complete routed triangle and failover test To practise an actual alternate path, use the spare G0/2 interfaces on R1 and R2 and add a third 2911-style router. This extends the OSPF variant; retain the existing VLAN/remote LAN design and do not restore the old static routes. New link/network Prefix First endpoint Second endpoint R1 G0/2 — R3 G0/0 10.44.0.180/30 R1 .181 R3 .182 R2 G0/2 — R3 G0/1 10.44.0.184/30 R2 .185 R3 .186 R3 G0/2 — additional test PC 10.44.0.224/28 R3 .225 gateway PC .226 These allocations do not overlap the original subnets. Give the additional PC mask 255.255.255.240 and gateway 10.44.0.225. On R1: configure terminal interface gigabitethernet 0/1 ip ospf cost 10 exit interface gigabitethernet 0/2 description TRANSIT_TO_R3 ip address 10.44.0.181 255.255.255.252 ip ospf cost 50 no shutdown exit router ospf 1 no passive-interface gigabitethernet 0/2 network 10.44.0.180 0.0.0.3 area 0 end On R2: configure terminal interface gigabitethernet 0/0 ip ospf cost 10 exit interface gigabitethernet 0/2 description TRANSIT_TO_R3 ip address 10.44.0.185 255.255.255.252 ip ospf cost 10 no shutdown exit router ospf 1 no passive-interface gigabitethernet 0/2 network 10.44.0.184 0.0.0.3 area 0 end On R3: enable configure terminal hostname R3 interface gigabitethernet 0/0 description TRANSIT_TO_R1 ip address 10.44.0.182 255.255.255.252 ip ospf cost 50 no shutdown exit interface gigabitethernet 0/1 description TRANSIT_TO_R2 ip address 10.44.0.186 255.255.255.252 ip ospf cost 10 no shutdown exit interface gigabitethernet 0/2 description ADDITIONAL_TEST_LAN ip address 10.44.0.225 255.255.255.240 no shutdown exit router ospf 1 router-id 3.3.3.3 passive-interface default no passive-interface gigabitethernet 0/0 no passive-interface gigabitethernet 0/1 network 10.44.0.180 0.0.0.3 area 0 network 10.44.0.184 0.0.0.3 area 0 network 10.44.0.224 0.0.0.15 area 0 end Verify that each router has two FULL neighbors. Explicit costs make the experiment independent of automatic bandwidth-derived cost on the transit links. R1 normally reaches R2's remote LAN over its cost-10 direct link instead of the cost-60 transit path through R3. R1 normally reaches R3's additional LAN through R2 (transit cost 20) instead of the direct cost-50 R1–R3 link. The advertised destination interface cost is added to these transit costs. Record the current show ip route next hops and a trace to both PCs. Shut only R1 G0/1 through its console. After link detection and OSPF convergence, the remote LAN should be reached through R3 via next hop .182. Expect a convergence interval and possible packet loss. Restore the interface with no shutdown, verify the adjacency returns and confirm that the lower-cost route is selected again. Do not assume the first trace accurately represents the converged state. Repeat using loss of R2 G0/2 while the direct R1–R2 link is working: the additional R3 LAN remains reachable over the more expensive R1–R3 link. Draw each path and distinguish link redundancy from failure of R1, which still owns every original VLAN gateway. This design still has single points of failure and is a teaching model rather than a production data centre architecture.

entries.title: 9. Apply a limited router ACL and understand its limits
entries.text: 9. Apply a limited router ACL and understand its limits Policy example: users in VLAN 10 may reach a lab web service on server .70 using TCP 80/443, but may not reach other VLAN 20 hosts, storage VLAN 30 or management VLAN 99. Other destinations remain allowed for this exercise. On R1: configure terminal ip access-list extended USERS_IN permit tcp 10.44.0.0 0.0.0.63 host 10.44.0.70 eq 80 permit tcp 10.44.0.0 0.0.0.63 host 10.44.0.70 eq 443 deny ip 10.44.0.0 0.0.0.63 10.44.0.64 0.0.0.63 deny ip 10.44.0.0 0.0.0.63 10.44.0.128 0.0.0.31 deny ip 10.44.0.0 0.0.0.63 10.44.0.160 0.0.0.15 permit ip 10.44.0.0 0.0.0.63 any exit interface gigabitethernet 0/0.10 ip access-group USERS_IN in end Rules are processed in order, first match wins, with an implicit deny at the end. The final permit is intentionally broad for other destinations; it is not a production least-privilege policy. The source restriction also drops packets using unexpected sources that fail to match any rule, but this does not replace a complete anti-spoofing design. Enable the simulated server's web service, then test browser access to .70. A ping to .70 is now supposed to fail: TCP web access is allowed while ICMP is denied. Verify counters with show access-lists USERS_IN and the binding/direction with show ip interface gigabitethernet 0/0.10. This is a stateless ingress ACL. It does not track sessions, and devices inside VLAN 10 can communicate locally without passing this routed interface. A TCP established ACL keyword checks selected TCP flags; it is not equivalent to a stateful connection table. Rollback: no ip access-group USERS_IN in under the same subinterface removes the binding. Confirm access and investigate the rules before deleting the ACL itself.

entries.title: 10. Stateful firewall lab with Linux namespaces
entries.text: 10. Stateful firewall lab with Linux namespaces This separate topology makes the firewall behaviour observable without depending on a commercial appliance image: az-client az-fw az-server 10.60.10.2/24 -- c0 : fwc 10.60.10.1 fws 10.60.20.1 : s0 -- 10.60.20.2/24 Use a dedicated disposable Linux VM. Do not replace the VM's host firewall or flush its ruleset. The nft commands below run only inside az-fw. If any of these namespace names already exist, choose different names consistently instead of deleting an unknown namespace. Build the topology Run the following commands one at a time and stop if any command fails. Resolve the failure before continuing. The veth pairs are created inside the newly created lab namespaces, so an existing host interface with a similar name is never moved. sudo ip netns add az-client sudo ip netns add az-fw sudo ip netns add az-server sudo ip -n az-client link add c0 type veth peer name fwc sudo ip -n az-client link set fwc netns az-fw sudo ip -n az-server link add s0 type veth peer name fws sudo ip -n az-server link set fws netns az-fw sudo ip -n az-client addr add 10.60.10.2/24 dev c0 sudo ip -n az-fw addr add 10.60.10.1/24 dev fwc sudo ip -n az-fw addr add 10.60.20.1/24 dev fws sudo ip -n az-server addr add 10.60.20.2/24 dev s0 sudo ip -n az-client link set lo up sudo ip -n az-fw link set lo up sudo ip -n az-server link set lo up sudo ip -n az-client link set c0 up sudo ip -n az-fw link set fwc up sudo ip -n az-fw link set fws up sudo ip -n az-server link set s0 up sudo ip -n az-client route add default via 10.60.10.1 sudo ip -n az-server route add default via 10.60.20.1 sudo ip netns exec az-fw sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 Before installing the firewall rules, verify sudo ip netns exec az-client ping -c 2 10.60.20.2. If it fails, resolve the routing/interface issue first. In two additional VM terminals, start these disposable test services and keep the terminals open: # Terminal A: the service that will be allowed. sudo ip netns exec az-server python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 10.60.20.2 # Terminal B: a working service that will deliberately be blocked. sudo ip netns exec az-server python3 -m http.server 8081 --bind 10.60.20.2 Python's development web server is a lab test service, not a production deployment. Confirm both URLs work from az-client before filtering. Using two running services avoids confusing a closed listening port with a firewall denial. Define the policy Allow new client-to-server TCP 8080 sessions. Permit established/related return traffic. Deny other forwarded traffic and unexpected traffic addressed to the firewall itself. This exercise is IPv4 only: the veth endpoints receive no routed IPv6 design and the inet policy also defaults to dropping unapproved IPv6 forwarding. sudo ip netns exec az-fw nft -f - <<'NFT' table inet az_lab { chain input { type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop; iifname "lo" accept ct state invalid drop ct state established,related accept } chain forward { type filter hook forward priority 0; policy drop; ct state invalid counter drop ct state established,related counter accept iifname "fwc" oifname "fws" ip saddr 10.60.10.0/24 ip daddr 10.60.20.2 tcp dport 8080 ct state new counter accept counter drop } chain output { type filter hook output priority 0; policy accept; } } NFT Run the load once. A second load of an identical table definition can conflict with or append to existing state depending on what is loaded; inspect it first. To replace this particular lab table, delete only table inet az_lab inside az-fw, then reload it. Do not issue a host-wide flush ruleset. sudo ip netns exec az-client curl --noproxy '*' --max-time 3 http://10.60.20.2:8080/ sudo ip netns exec az-client curl --noproxy '*' --max-time 3 http://10.60.20.2:8081/ sudo ip netns exec az-client ping -c 2 -W 1 10.60.20.2 sudo ip netns exec az-fw nft list table inet az_lab --noproxy '*' keeps these private lab requests on the direct namespace path even if the VM inherits HTTP proxy variables. Expected: 8080 returns an HTTP directory page; 8081 times out; ICMP echo receives no reply. The explicit drop counter increments for denied traffic. Established replies succeed because the connection tracker recognises the reverse traffic, not because a broad server-to-client allow rule was added. The input chain protects the firewall's own addresses. The forward chain controls traffic passing through it. Adding an SSH rule only to input would not permit SSH to a server behind it. A router doing no local DNS service should not receive arbitrary DNS queries just because clients need DNS elsewhere. Inspect the path sudo ip -n az-client route get 10.60.20.2 sudo ip -n az-fw route sudo ip -n az-fw neigh sudo ip netns exec az-server ss -lnt sudo ip netns exec az-fw tcpdump -ni fwc 'tcp port 8080 or tcp port 8081' route get should select the client interface and next hop 10.60.10.1. ss should show listeners on both test ports. Capture briefly while repeating a request; stop with Ctrl+C. Do not collect workplace traffic or secrets for this exercise. A packet capture on the client-side interface can see a denied SYN before it is dropped. Compare server-side fws if needed: seeing a frame at an ingress interface is not proof it was forwarded. NAT is a separate decision The namespace networks have working return routes, so they need no NAT. Address translation changes addressing; it is not an access-control rule and is not encryption. For a separate extension with a deliberately created external uplink named fwout, a masquerade rule could have the following shape: table ip az_nat { chain postrouting { type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept; oifname "fwout" ip saddr 10.60.10.0/24 masquerade } } Do not apply this fragment to the current two-interface lab: fwout does not exist. First design the external subnet, default route, explicit permitted forwarding, source translation and return path. Distinguish source NAT for outbound sessions from destination NAT/port forwarding for an inbound service. A destination NAT mapping alone must not accidentally grant access through the forwarding policy. Cleanup Stop the two Python servers using Ctrl+C in their own terminals and stop packet captures. Exit shells that are still inside a namespace. Then remove only the namespaces created for this exercise: sudo ip netns del az-client sudo ip netns del az-server sudo ip netns del az-fw The veth interfaces disappear with their namespaces. A namespace can remain alive while a process still holds it, which is why stopping the test services comes first. Confirm ip netns list no longer includes the lab names. No host interfaces, host firewall rules or host forwarding setting were changed by this procedure.

entries.title: 11. Translate the design to managed switches and firewalls
entries.text: 11. Translate the design to managed switches and firewalls NETGEAR managed switches Use the manual for the exact model and firmware. Unmanaged, smart managed and fully managed families do not expose identical features or syntax. A web UI feature name can differ from its Cisco counterpart. Discover the current management address through the approved local method and back up the configuration. Change credentials and configure a dedicated management VLAN/address with a recovery path. Create VLAN membership. Identify each access port's untagged membership and PVID; confirm that ingress classification and egress tagging agree. Mark uplinks as tagged members of the required VLANs. Match the peer's handling of native/untagged frames. Configure LACP on matching member ports at both ends; inspect the operational bundle. Set supported RSTP/MSTP behaviour deliberately. Do not assume it implements Cisco Rapid PVST+ identically. Limit management services/source networks, configure time/logging and verify access from the authorised admin host. Save persistent configuration and export a fresh backup after verification. A port in the correct VLAN membership table but with the wrong PVID can still put incoming untagged traffic into the wrong VLAN. Show both settings in your evidence. FortiGate and FortiSwitch FortiOS, hardware switch interfaces, software switches, VDOMs and FortiLink-managed switches have version-specific behaviour. Follow the installed release's administration guide. Do not attach an experimental FortiLink or HA configuration to an operational fabric. Translate each intended flow into a matrix before using the UI: Source zone Destination Service Decision Verification Lab users Designated web server HTTPS Allow Valid TLS/application response and policy log Lab users Management subnet Any Deny Failed test plus matching deny observation Admin host Switch management SSH/HTTPS as required Allow Named account and recorded successful login Application servers Approved DNS resolvers UDP/TCP 53 Allow if required Query and response, including TCP fallback test Untrusted zone Internal servers Unrequested new sessions Deny Explicit negative tests Then: Back up and record the release, operating mode and administrative recovery method. Define physical/VLAN interfaces, zones and connected addressing from the diagram. Verify routing and return routes; consider asymmetric paths that affect stateful inspection. Define address/service objects with clear ownership and purpose. Add the narrow required policies in the correct order, then verify the platform's default-deny behaviour. Decide explicitly whether NAT belongs on each flow. Internal segmentation often needs routing without translation. Enable suitable allowed/denied traffic logging without exposing sensitive payloads. Test allowed and denied traffic, inspect policy hits and the session view, then save evidence and a rollback point. FortiSwitch standalone management and FortiLink-managed configuration are different workflows. In a managed deployment, confirm where VLAN/port configuration is controlled before changing the switch directly. A GUI screenshot is not sufficient evidence of forwarding: test the path and inspect counters.

entries.title: 12. Linux network troubleshooting reference
entries.text: 12. Linux network troubleshooting reference Use these commands in a lab VM or the relevant namespace. Some tools/packages have different names between distributions. Read-only observation should come before a disruptive change. Question Linux command What to look for Is the interface present and up? ip -br link Administrative and link state; virtual NIC attachment Is the address/prefix correct? ip -br address Correct subnet, duplicate/unexpected addresses Which route will this destination use? ip route get 10.44.0.70 Selected interface, source and next hop Can the next hop resolve at Layer 2? ip neigh Reachable/stale entries vs repeated failed resolution Is the service listening? ss -lntup Bind address, port and protocol; elevated rights may reveal process details Is name resolution working? getent hosts example.com Application-facing resolution, including local policy What did a DNS resolver return? dig @<lab-resolver-ip> <lab-name> A Response code, answer, server and query time Is HTTPS working? curl -v --max-time 5 https://<lab-hostname>/ DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP stages; use the lab's trusted CA Is the firewall matching? sudo nft list ruleset Inspect host rules only when authorised; never flush to diagnose Are packets entering/leaving? sudo tcpdump -ni <lab-interface> host <lab-peer-ip> Direction, retransmissions and observable handshakes Did the service fail? systemctl status <lab-service> / journalctl -u <lab-service> Status, recent errors, timestamps and relevant logs Do not use curl -k as the default response to certificate errors. Check hostname, trust chain, validity period and system time. Do not paste verbose output containing tokens into public repositories. For a failure, record: symptom, affected scope, known working comparison, hypothesis, observation, one controlled change, result and rollback. Distinguish a DNS name failure from an IP routing failure and an HTTP error from a TCP connection failure.

entries.title: 13. Controlled fault exercises
entries.text: 13. Controlled fault exercises Use a saved simulator checkpoint. Introduce one fault at a time and write the expected evidence before testing. Injected fault Likely observation Confirmatory checks Recovery Server port assigned to VLAN 10 Server loses its intended gateway path Access VLAN, host mask/gateway, MAC table Restore VLAN 20 VLAN 99 omitted from Port-channel1 allowed list SW2 admin loses the R1 gateway and SW1 management path; its local SW2 management SVI remains reachable Trunk allowed/active VLANs on both peers Restore matching VLAN list through console Native VLAN mismatch Warnings and possible untagged traffic misclassification Native VLAN at both ends Restore native 999; inspect allowed list One LACP member shut Bundle remains usable with reduced member count EtherChannel flags and interface counters no shutdown, confirm rebundling Both LACP members shut SW2 becomes isolated from R1/SW1 Port-channel state and physical member state Restore at least one valid member Wrong /24 mask on server Some destinations work while others fail unexpectedly Compare exact subnet calculation and route selection Restore /26 R2 return route removed in static variant Outbound request may arrive but reply cannot return R2 route lookup, captures/trace Restore exact reverse route OSPF transit interface made passive Neighbor disappears and learned routes withdraw Passive list, adjacency, routing table Restore non-passive transit interface ACL web permit placed after a broader deny Required web session fails Ordered ACL and hit counters Reorder with narrow permits first Firewall allows input instead of forward Firewall management works, transit service fails Interface path and relevant chain counters Correct forward policy Service binds only to loopback Local request works; network request fails ss -lnt, bind address Bind intentionally to lab service address Wrong DNS record IP access works; name points elsewhere dig, resolver used, record/TTL Correct lab DNS record and observe cache behaviour Never resolve an access failure by repeatedly adding broad permit any rules without understanding which layer failed. In the simulator, restore the known working checkpoint if the experiment becomes unclear.

entries.title: 14. Design extension: resilient, segmented data centre network
entries.text: 14. Design extension: resilient, segmented data centre network Before adding commands, produce a design that answers these questions: Which traffic belongs in management, tenant/application, storage and backup networks? Which boundaries require a firewall? Where do default gateways live? Which links are Layer 2 and which are routed? Which device owns each IP address? What survives a single cable, NIC, power supply, switch, router or firewall failure? Which shared dependencies remain? Does the platform support the intended multi-chassis aggregation/stacking? Two independent switches cannot simply share a conventional LACP bundle without an appropriate supported mechanism. If using HSRP/VRRP, are the virtual IP, physical IPs, priorities, tracking and upstream paths defined? A first-hop redundancy protocol alone does not guarantee end-to-end reachability. Are MTU and encapsulation overhead consistent, especially for storage or overlay traffic? Jumbo frames need end-to-end support, not a single changed port. Are optics, fibre type, wavelength, speed, distance and connector polarity compatible? Do not look into a fibre or transceiver; follow the equipment handling procedure. Is time synchronised? Where do logs, SNMPv3/telemetry, configuration backups and alerts go? Who reviews failures and configuration drift? How will capacity be measured? Separate link speed, aggregate offered load, latency, loss and per-flow throughput. How will IPv6 be routed and filtered? Ignoring it does not establish that it is absent. Can a new operator recover management access and restore the last approved configuration? For a design review, include the physical diagram, logical VLAN/subnet map, routing design, flow matrix, management controls, failure matrix, monitoring plan, change sequence, validation and rollback. State simulator limitations and platform dependencies explicitly.

Completion evidence and reflection Create your own evidence rather than treating the expected results above as observations: Lab / date / simulator or OS version: Starting checkpoint and topology: Objective and expected required/prohibited flows: Address plan and calculations: Commands or changes made: Observed results and relevant counters: Fault introduced and explanation: Recovery and final verification: Remaining limitations / questions: Official sources consulted: What I would improve next time: Explain at least one successful application flow hop by hop, one blocked flow, one failure recovery and one residual single point of failure. Save sanitised configuration snippets rather than passwords or private infrastructure details.
